chapter_note.about: A finite automaton is a machine with a fixed, finite memory. This chapter starts with how to read a DFA and trace an NFA, then shows how an NFA becomes a DFA by the subset construction and how a DFA is shrunk to its minimal form. After that come regular expressions, converting a DFA to a regex, checking whether two expressions are equal, and the closure properties that tell you when a language is still regular. It ends with the product construction and with counting accepted strings. Most questions ask you to count minimal states or to pick the right regex.
chapter_note.simple: A finite automaton is like a vending machine: it can only remember a small, fixed amount about what you have pressed so far. You can draw one as a map of squares and arrows, and a word is accepted if reading it letter by letter leaves you on a finish square. The chapter teaches you to read such maps, to make an easy-to-draw version (an NFA) and convert it into the strict version (a DFA), and to shrink a map by gluing together squares that behave the same. It also covers regular expressions, which are short recipes for the same words. In exam words: DFA, NFA, subset construction, minimal DFA, regular expressions, closure properties, product construction and counting.

cards.title: DFA reading
cards.simple: A DFA is like a board game with one counter. You start on a marked square. Every letter of the input tells you exactly which square to move to, and you never get to choose. When the letters run out, you look at where your counter is standing. If the square is a special finish square, the word is accepted; otherwise it is rejected. In exam words: a DFA has exactly one move for every state and symbol, so a string has one run, and it is accepted when that run ends in a final state.
cards.idea: A **DFA** is a machine with a few states and one rule for every state and input symbol. Start in the start state, read the string one symbol at a time, and follow the single matching arrow each time. When the string ends, accept if you are standing in a final state.
cards.definition:
A DFA is a 5-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F).

- Q is the set of states and Σ is the alphabet.
- δ: Q × Σ → Q gives exactly one next state for each state and symbol.
- q0 is the start state and F ⊆ Q is the set of final states.

The run on w = w1 w2 … wn is q0, δ(q0, w1), δ(δ(q0, w1), w2), … The string is accepted when the last state is in F.
cards.intuition_full: The states are the machine's whole memory, so each state means something like 'what I still need to remember about the input so far'. Take the remainder example. After reading some bits, all that matters for divisibility by 3 is the remainder, and there are only three possible remainders, so three states are enough. Appending a bit b to a binary number turns the value v into 2v + b, which is why the new remainder is (2r + b) mod 3. A transition table and a drawn diagram carry the same information, so practise moving between them. If a drawn DFA has a missing arrow, there is a hidden dead state that swallows the string, and the string is rejected.

examples.setup: A DFA reads a binary number, most significant bit first, and keeps its remainder mod 3 in the states r0, r1, r2. The start state r0 is the only final state. Does it accept the string 1001?
steps: The state is the remainder mod 3 of the bits read so far. Reading bit b turns remainder r into (2r + b) mod 3. Start in r0 with input 1001.
Read 1: r0 goes to r1, because (2*0 + 1) mod 3 = 1.
Read 0: r1 goes to r2, because (2*1 + 0) mod 3 = 2.
Read 0: r2 goes to r1, because (2*2 + 0) mod 3 = 4 mod 3 = 1.
Read 1: r1 goes to r0, because (2*1 + 1) mod 3 = 0.
The string is used up and the run ended in r0, a final state, so 1001 is accepted. Check: 1001 is 9 in binary, and 9 = 3 * 3.
examples.answer: Accepted. The run is r0, r1, r2, r1, r0, which ends in the final state r0.

examples.setup: A DFA over {a, b} has start state p, final state r, and these moves: p on a goes to q, p on b stays at p; q on a goes to r, q on b goes to p; r loops on both a and b. Which strings does it accept?
steps: Name the states by what they remember. p: no pending a. q: the last symbol was an a that could start aa. r: aa has already appeared.
From q a b sends the run back to p, so an a followed by b is forgotten. Only two a's in a row reach r.
r loops on both symbols, so r is absorbing: once there, the string is accepted whatever follows.
Check two strings. baaab runs p, p, q, r, r, r and is accepted. abab runs p, q, p, q, p and is rejected.
examples.answer: Exactly the strings that contain aa as a substring.

examples.setup: Change one arrow of that DFA: r on b now goes to p instead of looping. What does it accept?
steps: Now r is no longer absorbing. After aa, a b sends the run back to p.
baaab runs p, p, q, r, r, p, ends in p, and is rejected, even though it contains aa.
The run is in r exactly when the last two symbols read were aa, and r is the only final state.
examples.answer: Exactly the strings that end in aa. One changed arrow turns 'contains' into 'ends with'.

cards.why: Every automata question starts with reading a machine correctly, and later cards (subset construction, minimising, products, closure) all produce or consume DFAs. In GATE: say what a drawn DFA accepts, or pick the regular expression that matches it.
how: Mark the start state (the arrow from nowhere) and the final states (double circles).
Follow exactly one arrow per symbol and write down the state after each symbol.
Accept only if the state after the last symbol is final.
To describe the language, name each state by what it remembers and check whether the final state is absorbing.
cards.mistake: Calling a language 'contains w' when it is really 'ends with w'. In a contains-DFA the final state loops on every symbol. If a final state has an arrow back to a non-final state, the machine checks a suffix instead. Also, only the state after the last symbol counts, not a final state visited on the way.
edge_cases: The empty string is accepted exactly when the start state is final.
A complete DFA over k symbols has |Q| × k arrows. A missing arrow means a hidden dead state.
Different pictures can accept the same language, as the minimal DFA card shows.
connections: An NFA relaxes 'exactly one move' to 'some path works' (next card).
Remainder DFAs like this one return in minimal-DFA counting, where counters multiply.

check.a: It is accepted, because the run on the empty string stays in the start state.

cards.title: NFA and ε-NFA
cards.simple: Picture a maze where, at some crossroads, you are allowed to split into several copies of yourself, and each copy walks a different path. Some doorways (the dashed ε ones) can be walked through for free, without using up a letter. The word is accepted if at least one copy ends up standing on a finish square. So instead of following one walker, you just keep a list of everywhere the copies could be after each letter. In exam words: an NFA accepts if some path ends in a final state, and in an ε-NFA you take the ε-closure before the first symbol and after every symbol.
cards.idea: An **NFA** may have several moves (or none) for a state and symbol. An **ε-NFA** may also move on ε without reading anything. To run one, keep the whole set of states you could be in, and accept if that set contains a final state at the end.
cards.definition:
An NFA is (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) where δ(q, a) is a set of states, possibly empty. For an ε-NFA, δ(q, ε) is allowed too.

- ε-closure(S) is S plus every state reachable from S using only ε arrows.
- Run: S0 = ε-closure({q0}). For each symbol a: S = ε-closure( the union of δ(q, a) over q in S ).
- Accept if the final S contains a state of F. If S ever becomes ∅, the run is dead and the string is rejected.
cards.intuition_full: The 'some path' rule means the machine can guess. For 'the second symbol from the right is a', the NFA just guesses when it has reached that symbol and then checks that exactly one more symbol follows. A DFA cannot guess, so it must remember a window of symbols instead. When you simulate an NFA by hand you are doing the same work a DFA would do: the set S is one DFA state. ε arrows only add free extra states, so you close the set before reading anything, and again after every symbol. Forgetting the closure after the last symbol is the classic loss of marks.

examples.setup: An ε-NFA has states A, B, C, D, start A, final D. Moves: A on b to A; A on ε to B; B on a to B and C; C on b to C; C on ε to D; D on a to D. Does it accept aab?
steps: An ε-NFA may also move along ε arrows (dashed) without reading a symbol. We track the set S of states we could be in. Input: aab, start state A.
Start with the ε-closure of A: A goes to B on ε, so S = {A, B}.
Read a: A has no a-move, B goes to B and C. Then close under ε: C goes to D. S = {B, C, D}.
Read a: B goes to B and C, D goes to D, and C has no a-move. The closure adds nothing new. S = {B, C, D}.
Read b: only C has a b-move, to C. Then close under ε: C goes to D. S = {C, D}.
The string is used up and S = {C, D} contains the final state D, so aab is accepted. Without that last closure you would see only {C} and wrongly reject.
examples.answer: Accepted. The sets are {A,B}, {B,C,D}, {B,C,D}, {C,D}, and the last one contains D.

examples.setup: An ε-NFA has states p, q, r, s with start p and final s. Moves: p on a to p; p on ε to q; q on b to r; r on ε to s. Does it accept ab?
steps: Start: ε-closure of {p} = {p, q}, because p goes to q on ε.
Read a: only p has an a-move, to p. Closure of {p} is {p, q}.
Read b: only q has a b-move, to r. The raw set is {r}.
Take the closure again: r goes to s on ε, so the set is {r, s}. It contains the final state s.
examples.answer: Accepted. Checking only {r} after the last symbol would wrongly reject. The language is a*b.

examples.setup: Same ε-NFA. Does it accept ba?
steps: Closure of {p} is {p, q}. Read b: q goes to r, closure gives {r, s}.
Read a: r has only an ε-move and s has no moves, so no state can read a. The set is ∅.
An empty set can never become non-empty, so the run is dead. s was in the set one symbol ago, but acceptance is judged after the last symbol.
examples.answer: Rejected. The sets are {p,q}, {r,s}, ∅.

cards.why: ε-NFAs are the stepping stone between a regular expression and a DFA, so tracing one is a core skill. In GATE: trace a small ε-NFA on a string, or read an NFA table before applying the subset construction.
how: Write S0 = the ε-closure of the start state.
For each symbol, take the union of the moves of every state in S, then take the ε-closure of the result.
If S becomes ∅, stop and reject.
After the last symbol, accept if S contains a final state.
cards.mistake: Skipping the ε-closure after the last symbol. A final state is often reachable only through an ε arrow, so the string looks rejected when it is accepted. The mirror mistake is to read an NFA as 'all paths must end final'. One good path is enough.
edge_cases: An NFA may have no move at all for a symbol. That path just dies.
ε-closure of a state always contains the state itself.
ε-cycles are harmless: the closure is a set, so each state is added once.
connections: The set S you track is exactly one state of the DFA built by the subset construction (next card).
Every regular expression has a simple ε-NFA, which is why regex and automata are equivalent.

check.q: What is ε-closure({q}) if q has no ε arrows?
check.a: {q}. A state always reaches itself.

check.q: An NFA is in the set {1, 3} and state 3 is final. The string has ended. Accept?
check.a: Yes. One final state in the set is enough.

check.q: Can an NFA be missing the transition for some state and symbol?
check.a: Yes. That path simply dies, and other paths may continue.

cards.title: Subset construction
cards.simple: An NFA is like a friend who can be in several places at once. A DFA is a friend who is only ever in one place, so to copy the NFA you invent places that mean 'the friend could be in rooms 0, 1 and 2 right now'. Each invented place is a set of rooms. You start from the starting set, see where each letter can take the set, and write down any new set you meet. You stop when no new set shows up. In exam words: the subset construction builds a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states, with at most 2^n of them, and only the reachable ones count.
cards.idea: Every NFA can be turned into a DFA whose states are **sets of NFA states**. Start from the start set, compute where each symbol sends a set, and add new sets as they appear. Stop when nothing new shows up. An n-state NFA gives at most 2^n DFA states, but usually far fewer are reachable.
cards.intuition_full: A DFA cannot guess, so it keeps track of every place the NFA could be. That list of places is the DFA state. The construction is a plain breadth-first search over sets, starting at {q0}. Because each set is a subset of n states, there are at most 2^n of them, and that is a ceiling, not the usual answer. Whether the ceiling is reached depends on the NFA. The 'k-th symbol from the right' languages hit it almost exactly, which is why they appear in GATE as hard examples. A set is final if it contains any NFA final state, because acceptance of the NFA needs just one good path.

examples.setup: NFA over {a, b}: state 0 (start) goes to 0 on a and on b, and to 1 on a. State 1 goes to 2 on a and on b. State 2 is final. Build the DFA by the subset construction.
steps: The NFA has states 0, 1, 2 (start 0, final 2). In the subset construction each DFA state is a SET of NFA states. We begin with the start set {0}.
From {0}: on a, state 0 goes to 0 and 1, so the set {0,1}. On b, state 0 goes to 0, so {0}. {0,1} is new.
From {0,1}: on a, 0 gives 0,1 and 1 gives 2, so {0,1,2}. On b, 0 gives 0 and 1 gives 2, so {0,2}. Two new sets.
From {0,1,2}: on a we get {0,1,2} again (state 2 has no moves). On b we get {0,2}. Nothing new appears.
From {0,2}: on a we get {0,1}, on b we get {0}. Both are known, so no new row is needed and the table is closed.
A set is final if it contains the NFA final state 2: {0,1,2} and {0,2}. Only 4 of the 2^3 = 8 possible subsets were reachable, so the DFA has 4 states.

examples.setup: L is the set of strings over {a, b} whose 4th symbol from the right is a. An NFA for L has 5 states. How many states does the minimal DFA need?
steps: The NFA: state 0 loops on a and b, goes to 1 on a, then 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 on any symbol. State 4 is final. That is 5 states.
After reading any string, the NFA's set is {0} plus every i in 1..4 such that the symbol i positions back was a. That depends on the last 4 symbols.
Each of the 2^4 = 16 patterns of the last four symbols gives a different set, and the sets are distinguishable, so the subset construction yields 16 states.
The ceiling for a 5-state NFA is 2^5 = 32, but state 0 is always in the set, so only 2^4 = 16 are reachable.
examples.answer: 16 states. The 2^n bound is a ceiling, and here the real count is 2^(n-1).

examples.setup: NFA: q0 goes to q1 on a, q1 goes to q2 on b, q2 is final, and no other moves exist. How many states does the complete DFA from the subset construction have?
steps: Start set {q0}. On a: {q1}. On b: no move, so ∅.
From {q1}: on a, ∅. On b, {q2}.
From {q2}: no moves, so a and b both give ∅. From ∅: ∅ on both.
The sets are {q0}, {q1}, {q2}, ∅: four states. ∅ is the dead state, and a complete DFA includes it.
examples.answer: 4 states, counting the dead state ∅.

cards.why: This is how NFA questions become DFA questions: sizes, minimal DFAs and complements all go through it. In GATE: bound the DFA size obtained from an n-state NFA, or count the reachable sets for a small NFA.
how: Write the start set (ε-closure of the start state).
For each new set and each symbol, take the union of the NFA moves, then the closure.
Add every new set as a row, and stop when no new set appears.
Mark final the sets that contain an NFA final state, then count the rows (including ∅ if it appears).
cards.mistake: Answering 2^n because the NFA has n states. 2^n is only an upper bound. Count the sets that are actually reachable from the start set, and then merge equivalent ones if the question asks for the minimal DFA.
edge_cases: The smallest possible DFA from any NFA has 1 state, for example for the language Σ*.
∅ appears as a DFA state whenever some symbol can leave the NFA with no move, and it counts as a state of a complete DFA.
An NFA with n states can force 2^n DFA states in the worst case, but that needs special constructions.
connections: Minimising the resulting DFA (next card) is how the question 'size of the minimal DFA' is answered.
Regular expressions become ε-NFAs, and the subset construction turns them into DFAs: this is the full pipeline.

check.q: An NFA has 5 states. What is the largest number of DFA states the subset construction can give?
check.a: 2^5 = 32, counting the empty set.

check.q: Which subsets are final in the DFA?
check.a: Every subset that contains at least one final state of the NFA.

check.q: Can the DFA built from an NFA have fewer states than the NFA?
check.a: Yes. Only reachable sets count, and for some NFAs there are only a few.

A set is final if it contains the NFA final state 2: {0,1,2} and {0,2}. Only 4 of the 2^3 = 8 possible subsets were reachable, so the DFA has 4 states.

cards.what: Every NFA can be turned into a DFA whose states are **sets of NFA states**. Start from the start set, compute where each symbol sends a set, and add new sets as they appear. Stop when nothing new shows up. An n-state NFA gives at most 2^n DFA states, but usually far fewer are reachable.

Given an NFA N with n states, the DFA D has:

- states: subsets of Q (only the reachable ones are kept);
- start state: ε-closure({q0});
- transition: δD(S, a) = ε-closure( union of δ(q, a) for q in S );
- final states: every set S that contains at least one final state of N.

The empty set ∅ is a legal DFA state: it is the dead state.

**Worked example.** NFA over {a, b}: state 0 (start) goes to 0 on a and on b, and to 1 on a. State 1 goes to 2 on a and on b. State 2 is final. Build the DFA by the subset construction.

1. The NFA has states 0, 1, 2 (start 0, final 2). In the subset construction each DFA state is a SET of NFA states. We begin with the start set {0}.
2. From {0}: on a, state 0 goes to 0 and 1, so the set {0,1}. On b, state 0 goes to 0, so {0}. {0,1} is new.
3. From {0,1}: on a, 0 gives 0,1 and 1 gives 2, so {0,1,2}. On b, 0 gives 0 and 1 gives 2, so {0,2}. Two new sets.
4. From {0,1,2}: on a we get {0,1,2} again (state 2 has no moves). On b we get {0,2}. Nothing new appears.
5. From {0,2}: on a we get {0,1}, on b we get {0}. Both are known, so no new row is needed and the table is closed.
6. A set is final if it contains the NFA final state 2: {0,1,2} and {0,2}. Only 4 of the 2^3 = 8 possible subsets were reachable, so the DFA has 4 states.

**Answer:** 4 DFA states: {0}, {0,1}, {0,1,2}, {0,2}. The finals are {0,1,2} and {0,2}.

cards.title: Minimal DFA and counting states
cards.simple: Suppose two friends in a queue would always react in exactly the same way to anything you say to them, now and forever. You do not need both of them, so you can replace the pair with one friend. Minimising a DFA is the same: find states that behave identically for every possible future input, and glue them into one. You do it by sorting states into groups and splitting a group whenever two members send you to different groups. In exam words: the minimal DFA merges states that no string can distinguish, and you can find it by partition refinement.
cards.idea: Two DFA states are **equivalent** if every string leads both to final or both to non-final. Equivalent states can be merged. Start with two groups, final and non-final, and split any group whose members send a symbol to different groups. When nothing splits, each group is one state of the **minimal DFA**.
cards.definition:
States p and q are distinguishable if some string w makes exactly one of δ(p, w), δ(q, w) final. The minimal DFA for L is unique up to renaming and has one state for each class of indistinguishable states (and only reachable states are kept).

Partition refinement (Hopcroft's method):

1. Start with {final states} and {non-final states}.
2. Split a group if two members go to different groups on some symbol.
3. Repeat until no group splits. Each final group becomes one state.
cards.intuition_full: A state is really a promise about the future: 'from here, these strings will be accepted'. Two states with the same promise are interchangeable. The refinement works from the end of the string backwards: final versus non-final separates states by the empty string, then states that reach different groups after one symbol are separated by that symbol plus the old reason, and so on. This is why the algorithm only ever splits and never merges. Remove unreachable states first, and keep a dead state in a complete DFA: it is a real state whose future is 'never accept'. For counters, states are residue tuples, and tuples that cannot be told apart merge.

examples.setup: A 5-state DFA over {a, b}: A on a goes to B, A on b stays at A; B on a goes to C, B on b goes to D; D on a goes to E, D on b goes to B; C and E loop on both symbols and are the final states. Find the minimal DFA.
steps: This DFA has 5 states. Two states can merge only if no string tells them apart. Start with the coarsest split: final states {C, E} (class F) versus the rest {A, B, D} (class N).
For each state, write the classes its a-move and b-move lead to. A: (N,N). B: (F,N). D: (F,N). C and E: (F,F).
Inside class N, A differs from B and D: A's a-move stays in N, theirs go to F. So N splits into {A} (class P) and {B, D} (class Q). {C, E} stays together as R.
Check again with the new classes. A: (Q,P). B: (R,Q). D: (R,Q). C: (R,R). E: (R,R). States in the same class have the same pair, so nothing splits.
The partition is stable. B and D are equivalent, and so are C and E. Merge each pair into one state.
The minimal DFA has 3 states: {A}, {B,D}, {C,E}. It counts the a's up to 2: strings with at least two a's.
examples.answer: 3 states: {A}, {B,D}, {C,E}. The language is 'at least two a's'.

examples.setup: Over {a, b}, L = {w : #a(w) mod 4 = 2 and #b(w) is even}. What is the minimum number of DFA states?
steps: A DFA can track the pair (#a mod 4, #b mod 2). That gives 4 × 2 = 8 states, and all are reachable.
The only accepting pair is (2, 0). To tell two pairs (i, j) and (i', j') apart, append the string that would take the first to (2, 0): a's to fix the first coordinate and a b if j is odd.
That string accepts from (i, j) but not from any other pair, so every pair is distinguishable from every other.
No merging is possible, so the minimal DFA has all 8 states.
examples.answer: 8 states. When the accepting set is a single pair, counters multiply with no merging.

examples.setup: Over {a, b}, L = {w : #a(w) mod 6 is 0 or 3}. How many states does the minimal DFA need?
steps: The obvious DFA keeps #a mod 6, which is 6 states. Accepting residues: 0 and 3.
Residues 0 and 3 are equivalent: adding any a's gives 1, 4, ... versus 4, 1, ... and the accept pattern repeats with period 3.
In general residues i and i + 3 behave the same, so the 6 states collapse to 3 classes: {0,3}, {1,4}, {2,5}.
Check: the language is 'number of a's divisible by 3', which clearly needs only 3 states.
examples.answer: 3 states. The accepting set has period 3, so the period (not the modulus) sets the count.

cards.title: Regular expressions
cards.simple: A regular expression is a recipe for building words out of three moves. You can pick one of two options (the plus sign means 'or'), you can repeat something as many times as you like including zero (the star), or you can put two things one after the other. To understand a recipe, start with the smallest bracket, work out the few words it makes, then see what the star does with them, then add the end. To check a recipe against a description, just try two or three short words on it. In exam words: + is union, * is Kleene star, concatenation is juxtaposition, and ∅* = {ε}.
cards.idea: A **regular expression** describes a set of strings using three operations: union (+), concatenation (writing parts side by side), and star (*, repeat zero or more times). Read it from the inside out, and when you are unsure, test two or three short strings.
cards.intuition_full: Think of each operator as a way to combine sets of strings. Union pours two sets together, concatenation glues one string from each, and the star glues any number of strings from one set. Because the star allows zero repeats, R* always contains the empty string, even if R itself does not. The same set often has several expressions, so pick-the-regex questions are usually solved by describing the language in words first and then testing short strings: one string that should be in and one that should be out kills most options. The symbol + in GATE regexes is union, not 'one or more'.

examples.setup: Describe the language of the regular expression (ab + b)* a, and test the strings abba and abab.
steps: Read R = (ab + b)* a from the inside out. + means OR, * means 'repeat zero or more times', and writing two parts next to each other means 'then'.
The union ab + b is the set of two blocks: {ab, b}.
The star repeats blocks zero or more times, in any mix: ε (zero blocks), b, ab, bb, abb, bab, bbb, and so on.
Put an a after every string of the star part: a, ba, aba, bba, abba, baba, bbba, and so on. That is L(R).
Test two strings. abba = (ab)(b)(a) is in L(R). abab is not: it does not end in a, and every string of L(R) ends with the single trailing a.
In words: L(R) is the set of strings that end in a and contain no aa. Every a inside the blocks is followed by b, and only the final a is free.
examples.answer: L = strings that end in a and contain no aa. abba is in L, abab is not.

examples.setup: Which regular expression describes the set of strings over {a, b} with exactly one b? (A) a*ba*   (B) a*b*a*   (C) (a+b)*b(a+b)*   (D) a*b
steps: Describe the language: some a's, one b, some a's. So a*ba* looks right.
Test b: in the language (A matches it with zero a's on each side).
Test bb, which has two b's and so is not in the language. (B) a*b*a* matches bb, so B is out. (C) also matches bb, so C is out.
Test ba, which has exactly one b. (D) a*b cannot match it because it must end in b, so D is out.
examples.answer: (A) a*ba*. Option (B) allows any number of b's in a block, (C) allows any number of b's in total, and (D) forces the b to be last.

examples.setup: What is the language of a*(∅ + b)∅* ? And of a*∅ ?
steps: ∅ + b is the union of the empty set with {b}, so it is {b}.
∅* = {ε}: zero repeats of anything gives ε, even for the empty set.
For a*∅: gluing any string to a string of the empty set is impossible, so concatenating with ∅ gives ∅.
examples.answer: a*b for the first and ∅ for the second.

cards.title: DFA to regex
cards.simple: Imagine a small town with two squares joined by roads, and every road is signposted with a letter. You want one sentence that describes every walk that starts at home and ends at a finish square. The trick is to bulldoze one square at a time. When a square disappears, any walk that used to pass through it becomes a single new road whose sign lists everything you would have read on the way. Repeat until one loop is left, and the loop's signs are your answer. In exam words: state elimination replaces paths through a removed state with regex labels, and in practice you describe the language in words first.
cards.idea: To turn a DFA into a regular expression, remove its states one by one. When you remove a state, every path **into it, around its loop, and out of it** becomes a new arrow labelled with a regex. In exams you can often skip the algorithm: say what the DFA accepts in words and write a regex for that.
cards.definition:
State elimination: add a new start and a new final state if needed. To remove a state q, for every pair (p, r) with arrows p → q and q → r replace them with an arrow p → r labelled

  (label p→q) (label q→q)* (label q→r),

then merge parallel arrows with +. When only start and final remain, the label between them is the regex.

Shortcut: describe the language in words, then check the regex on short strings.
cards.intuition_full: Every accepted string is a walk through the machine. Removing a state does not change which walks exist, it just writes them in bulk: 'enter by x, spin on the loop y as long as you like, leave by z' is x y* z. Parallel arrows are alternatives, so they join with +. The final label between start and final is the union of all walks. The result is never unique, so two correct answers may look different. This is why GATE gives options and expects you to test strings. Describing the DFA in words ('even number of a's') usually tells you the regex immediately, for example b*(ab*ab*)*: b's anywhere, a's in pairs.

examples.setup: The DFA with states E (start, final) and O has E on a to O, E on b to E, O on a to E, and O on b to O. It accepts strings with an even number of a's. Find a regular expression for it.
steps: This DFA accepts strings with an even number of a's. State E (start, final) means 'even so far', O means 'odd so far'. We will remove O and keep the regex on the arrows.
Look at the detour E → O → E. It reads an a, then any number of b's (the loop on O), then an a. As a regex that is a b* a.
Remove state O and put the detour on E as a new loop labelled ab*a.
Two parallel loops merge into one with +. E now has a single loop labelled b + ab*a.
E is both the start and the only final state, so we go round that loop any number of times: (b + ab*a)*.
Check: baab = b, then a·ε·a, then b is in the language (two a's). ab has one a, so it is out. Brute force over all strings up to length 10 confirms the regex matches the DFA.
examples.answer: (b + ab*a)*, which also equals b*(ab*ab*)*.

examples.setup: A DFA has states r0 (start, final), r1, r2. Every b loops on the current state, and a moves r0 to r1 to r2 to r0. Which regex describes it?
steps: In words: the number of a's is a multiple of 3 and the b's can be anywhere.
b's anywhere: b*. A group of three a's with b's between and after: a b* a b* a b*.
Any number of groups: b* (ab*ab*ab*)*.
Test: aaa is accepted (one group of three). abab has two a's and is rejected. baaab has three a's and is accepted, by the machine and the regex alike.
examples.answer: b*(ab*ab*ab*)*. An equivalent form is (b + ab*ab*a)*.

examples.setup: For the even-a's DFA, is b*(ab*ab*)* the same language as (b + ab*a)* ?
steps: Both describe 'even number of a's'. In the first, b's come anywhere and the a's are paired up with b's allowed between and after each pair.
In the second, each iteration is either a b or a pair of a's with b's between them.
Brute force over every string of length up to 10 shows they agree on all of them.
examples.answer: Yes, they are equal. State elimination can produce different-looking regexes for the same DFA.

Write the regex from the words: loops become stars, exits become concatenation.
Test one string that should be accepted and one that should not on each option.

cards.mistake: Dropping the loop of the removed state. A path through q reads x then y* then z, not just x z. The second slip is to forget to merge parallel arrows with +.
edge_cases: If a state has no loop, y* is just ε and drops out.
A dead state is removed first: no accepted walk uses it.
The regex may be much longer than the language's description, but it is correct.
connections: Regex to ε-NFA to DFA is the other direction, so regexes and DFAs are equivalent.

cards.title: Equivalence and witnesses
cards.simple: Two cooks both say they make the same soup. To prove they do not, you only need one spoonful where the taste is different. To believe they do, you would have to taste every possible spoonful, which is impossible, so instead you use a smarter test. For regexes, you try short strings in order of length and look for one that one recipe makes and the other cannot. For machines, you run both together and look for a moment where one says yes and the other says no. In exam words: two languages are different when some witness string is in exactly one of them, and equality of regular languages is decidable using the product construction.
cards.idea: To show two regular expressions are **different**, find one string that one accepts and the other rejects (a **witness**). Test short strings first. To show two DFAs are **equal**, run them together as a product and check that no reachable pair has one final and one non-final state.
cards.definition:

For DFAs M1 and M2: build the product, mark a pair final when exactly one component is final, and test whether any marked pair is reachable. If none is, the languages are equal. Any reachable marked pair gives a shortest witness: the path to it.

For regexes: use algebra (for example (ab)*a = a(ba)*, (a*b*)* = (a + b)*) or find a witness.
cards.intuition_full: Equality of two infinite sets sounds hard, but regular languages are finite objects: machines with finitely many states. Equal pairs are the ones that survive the tests and are covered by an identity. To prove equality you need an identity or the product test, not just a handful of passing strings.

Length 0 and 1: ε is in neither. a is in both: (ab)*a with zero repeats, a(ab)* with zero repeats.
Length 2: aa and ab are in neither expression. Both languages contain only a so far.
Length 3: aab = a·(ab) is in a(ab)* but not in (ab)*a, because that one must end in a. A witness: the two languages differ.
aba = (ab)·a is in (ab)*a but not in a(ab)*. Another witness, on the other side. One witness is enough.
So (ab)*a ≠ a(ab)*. Compare a(ba)*: it generates a, aba, ababa, the same strings as (ab)*a, and no string up to length 8 separates them. Those two are equal.

cards.title: Closure properties
cards.simple: Think of regular languages as a club with strict rules about what its members can do. If you take two members and combine them in the allowed ways (put their words together, glue them end to end, repeat them, flip a yes into a no, or ask for words both accept), the result is still a member. For complement it is easy to see why: take the machine, swap the finish squares with the non-finish squares, and it now accepts exactly the words it used to reject. The rules break when you combine infinitely many languages, or when you take a random part of a language. In exam words: regular languages are closed under union, intersection, complement, difference, reversal, concatenation and star, but not under infinite union or arbitrary subsets.
cards.idea: Applying certain operations to **regular languages** always gives a regular language. Union, intersection, complement, difference, concatenation, star, reversal and prefix are all safe. Infinite unions and taking an arbitrary subset are not. For complement, make the DFA complete and **swap final and non-final states**.
cards.intuition_full: Each safe operation has a construction on automata that keeps the memory finite. Complement flips the verdict of a DFA, so it needs no new states. Union and intersection run two DFAs together (product). Concatenation and star glue NFAs with ε arrows. Reversal reads the machine backwards. Unsafe cases come from needing unbounded memory: an infinite union can glue together a family such as {a^n b^n}, each finite and so regular, but their union needs to count. A random subset of a regular language can be anything, because Σ* is regular and contains every language over Σ.

examples.setup: L is the set of strings over {a, b} containing bb. A complete DFA for L has states s0 (start), s1, s2 with s0 on a to s0, s0 on b to s1, s1 on a to s0, s1 on b to s2, and s2 absorbing. Build a DFA for the complement of L and test abb and aba.
steps: L = strings that contain bb. This complete DFA has the single final state s2, which absorbs everything once bb has appeared.
Run abb on M: s0, s0, s1, s2. It ends in the final state s2, so abb is accepted. It does contain bb.
Complement: keep every arrow and swap final with non-final. Now s0 and s1 are final, and s2 is not.
Run abb on the new machine: it still ends in s2, which is no longer final, so abb is rejected. That is right, because abb contains bb.
Run aba on the new machine: s0, s0, s1, s0. It ends in s0, which is now final, so aba is accepted. aba contains no bb.

This works because the DFA is complete: every string ends somewhere. With a missing arrow the dead state is invisible and flipping would miss it. Closure under complement then gives intersection and difference by De Morgan.
examples.answer: Make s0 and s1 final and s2 non-final. abb is rejected and aba is accepted: the machine now accepts exactly the strings with no bb.

examples.setup: L is regular and L' is an arbitrary language over {a, b}. Which of these must be regular? (i) L ∩ L'   (ii) L ∪ {w : |w| ≤ 3}   (iii) the reversal of L   (iv) the complement of L   (v) any subset of L
steps: (i) Take L = Σ* (regular) and L' = {a^n b^n}. Then L ∩ L' = L', which is not regular. So (i) need not be regular.
(ii) A finite language is regular, and the union of two regular languages is regular. So (ii) is regular.
(iii) Reverse the arrows of a DFA for L: reversal keeps regularity. So (iii) is regular.
(iv) Complement is closed. (v) Fails: every language over {a, b} is a subset of Σ*, which is regular, and {a^n b^n} is not.
examples.answer: (ii), (iii) and (iv) must be regular. (i) and (v) need not be.

examples.setup: For each n, the language {a^n b^n} has a single string, so it is regular. Is the infinite union over all n ≥ 0, that is {a^n b^n : n ≥ 0}, regular?
steps: Each single-string language is regular, since a finite language is regular.
The union over all n is the language {a^n b^n}. A DFA would have to count the a's to match the b's, which needs infinitely many states.
So the union is not regular, even though each piece is. Closure holds for finite unions only.
examples.answer: Not regular. Regular languages are closed under finite union, not infinite union.

For an operation with an arbitrary language, test a counterexample such as L = Σ* and L' = {a^n b^n}.
Finite languages are always regular, and removing or adding finitely many strings keeps regularity.
Infinite unions and arbitrary subsets are the usual traps.
cards.mistake: Believing that a subset or a part of a regular language is regular, or that an infinite union of regular languages is regular. Another slip is flipping the finals of an incomplete DFA, which misses the implicit dead state.

L ∩ L' with L regular and L' arbitrary can be non-regular (L = Σ*).
Complement of L over Σ needs the alphabet Σ fixed: it is Σ* − L.

cards.title: Product construction
cards.simple: Imagine two referees watching the same match, one counting fouls by team A and one counting fouls by team B, and each only cares whether their count is odd or even. To know what both think at once, you keep a little card with two boxes, one for each referee, and update both boxes after every whistle. The card is now a single state, and you only need to decide which cards count as 'both happy' or 'at least one happy' to answer different questions. In exam words: the product DFA has pairs of states, runs both machines in lockstep, and the final pairs depend on whether you want intersection, union or difference.
cards.idea: To combine two DFAs M1 and M2, run them **in lockstep**. A state of the product is a pair (p, q), and a symbol moves both parts. Only the choice of final pairs changes with the operation: both final for intersection, either final for union.
cards.intuition_full: The product remembers everything both machines remember. Since each machine reads the same input, the pair evolves exactly as the two originals would, side by side. The final set is where the logic lives: 'both accept' gives AND, 'at least one accepts' gives OR, 'one accepts, the other does not' gives difference or symmetric difference. That is also why union and intersection preserve regularity: the product is a DFA with finitely many states. The number |Q1| × |Q2| is a ceiling. If the two machines are correlated, for example both tracking the parity of a's, only a few pairs are ever reached, and after minimising the count can be smaller still.

examples.setup: D1 accepts strings over {a, b} with an even number of a's, and D2 accepts strings with an even number of b's. Build the product DFA and mark its final states for 'both even' (intersection) and for 'at least one even' (union).
steps: Run D1 (even number of a's) and D2 (even number of b's) at the same time. A product state is a pair: (a-parity, b-parity), written e or o for even or odd. Start: both even, ee.
From ee: reading a flips only the first part, so oe. Reading b flips only the second part, so eo.
From oe: a gives ee, b gives oo.
From eo: a gives oo, b gives ee.
From oo: a gives eo, b gives oe. No new pairs appear: all 2 × 2 = 4 pairs are reachable.
Intersection (both even): the pair is final only if both parts are final, so just ee.
Union (at least one even): the pair is final if either part is final: ee, oe and eo. Same states and arrows, different finals.
examples.answer: 4 states ee, oe, eo, oo. Intersection: final = {ee}. Union: final = {ee, oe, eo}.

examples.setup: D1 counts #a mod 3 (accepting residue 0) and D2 counts #b mod 2 (accepting residue 0). What is the minimum number of states of a DFA for the intersection?
steps: The product has 3 × 2 = 6 pairs. a changes the first part, b the second, so all 6 are reachable.
The only final pair is (0, 0). Every other pair can reach (0, 0) by a specific string, and different pairs need different strings.
So no two pairs are equivalent: appending the right string accepts from exactly one pair.
No merging is possible.
examples.answer: 6 states. Counters on different symbols multiply.

examples.setup: D1 and D2 both accept strings with an even number of a's (they track the same parity). How many states of the product DFA are reachable?
steps: Start (0, 0). Reading a flips both parts together: (1, 1), then back to (0, 0). Reading b changes nothing.
The pairs (0, 1) and (1, 0) can never occur, because both parts always equal each other.
Only 2 of the 4 pairs are reachable, so the product has 2 states.
examples.answer: 2 reachable pairs, not 4. |Q1| × |Q2| is only an upper bound.

cards.why: Union, intersection and difference of regular languages are proved with the product, and size questions ask how many states it has. In GATE: states of a product DFA, or a minimal DFA for a combined condition on counters.

Start from (start1, start2) and keep only the reachable pairs.
Choose the final pairs from the operation: AND, OR or difference.
To count the minimal DFA, merge pairs with equal futures.

Difference L1 − L2 marks pairs with the first part final and the second non-final.
The product of an n-state and an m-state DFA needs at most n m states, and this bound can be reached.

cards.what_full:
To combine two DFAs M1 and M2, run them **in lockstep**. A state of the product is a pair (p, q), and a symbol moves both parts. Only the choice of final pairs changes with the operation: both final for intersection, either final for union.

Given DFAs M1 = (Q1, Σ, δ1, s1, F1) and M2 = (Q2, Σ, δ2, s2, F2) over the same alphabet, the product has:

- states Q1 × Q2 (only reachable pairs matter);
- start (s1, s2);
- δ((p, q), a) = (δ1(p, a), δ2(q, a));
- final pairs: F1 × F2 for ∩, pairs with p ∈ F1 or q ∈ F2 for ∪, p ∈ F1 and q ∉ F2 for difference.

The product has at most |Q1| × |Q2| states.

**Worked example.** D1 accepts strings over {a, b} with an even number of a's, and D2 accepts strings with an even number of b's. Build the product DFA and mark its final states for 'both even' (intersection) and for 'at least one even' (union).

1. Run D1 (even number of a's) and D2 (even number of b's) at the same time. A product state is a pair: (a-parity, b-parity), written e or o for even or odd. Start: both even, ee.
2. From ee: reading a flips only the first part, so oe. Reading b flips only the second part, so eo.
3. From oe: a gives ee, b gives oo.
4. From eo: a gives oo, b gives ee.
5. From oo: a gives eo, b gives oe. No new pairs appear: all 2 × 2 = 4 pairs are reachable.
6. Intersection (both even): the pair is final only if both parts are final, so just ee.
7. Union (at least one even): the pair is final if either part is final: ee, oe and eo. Same states and arrows, different finals.

**Answer:** 4 states ee, oe, eo, oo. Intersection: final = {ee}. Union: final = {ee, oe, eo}.
cards.why_full:
Union, intersection and difference of regular languages are proved with the product, and size questions ask how many states it has. In GATE: states of a product DFA, or a minimal DFA for a combined condition on counters.

cards.trap: Reporting |Q1| × |Q2| without checking reachability, or marking the wrong pairs final. For union, a pair is final if either part is final, not both. Also, both DFAs must be over the same alphabet and complete.

cards.title: Counting accepted strings
cards.simple: Suppose a crowd of people walks through a maze, and at every junction each person splits into one copy for each letter. Instead of following each person, you stand at each room and just count how many people are in it after each step. At the start there is one person in the first room. After every step each room's count is the sum of what the arrows pointing into it bring. When the walk is over, add up the counts of the finish rooms. In exam words: count accepted strings of a given length by dynamic programming over the DFA states, or with binomials or inclusion-exclusion.
cards.idea: To count the strings of length n that a DFA accepts, track **how many strings end in each state** after each length. Start with 1 in the start state. At each step every string extends by each symbol, so a state's new count is the sum over incoming arrows. After n steps add up the final states' counts.
cards.intuition_full: Every string of length n corresponds to exactly one run, so counting strings is counting runs, and the DFA keeps all runs separate by state. Counting by state is dynamic programming: the number of ways to be in t after k+1 symbols uses only the numbers after k symbols. The row sums are always 2^k for a complete DFA over two symbols, a handy check. For counter conditions the DFA is just a mod counter, so the count collapses into a sum of binomial coefficients. For 'or' conditions, count each condition and subtract the overlap (inclusion-exclusion), or complement and count the strings that avoid the pattern.

examples.setup: A DFA over {a, b} has states s0 (start), s1, s2 (final): s0 on a to s1, s0 on b to s0; s1 on a to s1, s1 on b to s2; s2 loops on both symbols. How many strings of length 5 does it accept?
steps: Count the strings of length 5 over {a, b} that contain ab. Instead of listing 32 strings, count how many strings of each length end in each state. At length 0, one empty string sits in s0.
Length 1: from s0, b stays in s0 (1 string) and a goes to s1 (1 string). Counts 1, 1, 0.
Length 2: s0 = 1 (via b). s1 = 1 + 1 = 2 (a from s0, a from s1). s2 = 1 (b from s1) + 2 × 0. Counts 1, 2, 1.
Length 3: s0 = 1, s1 = 1 + 2 = 3, s2 = 2 (b from s1) + 2 × 1 (both symbols from s2) = 4. Counts 1, 3, 4.
Accepted strings of length 5 are those that end in the final state s2: 26. Check: the 6 strings with no ab are b^i a^j, and 32 − 6 = 26.
examples.answer: 26 strings (all strings of length 5 that contain ab).

examples.setup: How many binary strings of length 7 have a number of 1s divisible by 4?
steps: The condition depends only on the count of 1s, so choose which positions hold 1s: C(7, j) strings with j ones.
j must be 0 or 4 (j ≤ 7 and j divisible by 4).
examples.answer: 36 strings. A mod-counter condition becomes a sum of binomials.

examples.setup: How many strings of length 6 over {a, b} start with a or end with b?
steps: Starting with a: the first symbol is fixed, 2^5 = 32 strings. Ending with b: 2^5 = 32.
Both at once: first fixed and last fixed, 2^4 = 16 strings.
Inclusion-exclusion: 32 + 32 − 16 = 48. Check by the complement: starts with b and ends with a gives 2^4 = 16, and 64 − 16 = 48.
examples.answer: 48 strings. Adding the two counts without subtracting the overlap would give 64.

cards.why: Counting questions look like combinatorics but are solved cleanly with the automaton. In GATE: count strings of a given length accepted by a DFA, or strings with a mod-count condition.
how: Write the DFA states as columns and the lengths 0, 1, 2, ... as rows.
Start with 1 in the start state and fill each next row from the incoming arrows.
Check that each row sums to the total number of strings of that length.
Add the final states' counts in row n. For counter conditions or OR conditions, use binomials or inclusion-exclusion.
cards.mistake: Adding the counts of two overlapping conditions without subtracting what they share, or counting runs that pass through a dead state. Also, each arrow with two labels (a, b) counts twice for the target state.
edge_cases: Length 0: the answer is 1 if the start state is final, else 0.
Absorbing final states keep accumulating: s2 receives 2 × its previous count each step.
Dead states are columns whose count never matters for the answer.
connections: The same table method counts accepted strings for the product DFA (Card 9).
Probability questions on random bit strings reduce to the same counts.

check.q: Each row of counts for a complete DFA over {a, b} must add up to what?
check.a: 2^n, the total number of strings of length n.

cards.what_full:
To count the strings of length n that a DFA accepts, track **how many strings end in each state** after each length. Start with 1 in the start state. At each step every string extends by each symbol, so a state's new count is the sum over incoming arrows. After n steps add up the final states' counts.

Let c_k(s) be the number of strings of length k whose run ends in state s. Then

  c_0(start) = 1, c_0(s) = 0 otherwise;
  c_{k+1}(t) = sum over (s, a) with δ(s, a) = t of c_k(s);
  answer = sum of c_n(f) for f in F.

For 'number of 1s is r mod m' conditions, the answer is the sum of C(n, j) over j ≡ r (mod m).

**Worked example.** A DFA over {a, b} has states s0 (start), s1, s2 (final): s0 on a to s1, s0 on b to s0; s1 on a to s1, s1 on b to s2; s2 loops on both symbols. How many strings of length 5 does it accept?

1. Count the strings of length 5 over {a, b} that contain ab. Instead of listing 32 strings, count how many strings of each length end in each state. At length 0, one empty string sits in s0.
2. Length 1: from s0, b stays in s0 (1 string) and a goes to s1 (1 string). Counts 1, 1, 0.
3. Length 2: s0 = 1 (via b). s1 = 1 + 1 = 2 (a from s0, a from s1). s2 = 1 (b from s1) + 2 × 0. Counts 1, 2, 1.
4. Length 3: s0 = 1, s1 = 1 + 2 = 3, s2 = 2 (b from s1) + 2 × 1 (both symbols from s2) = 4. Counts 1, 3, 4.
5. Length 4: s0 = 1, s1 = 1 + 3 = 4, s2 = 3 + 2 × 4 = 11. Counts 1, 4, 11.
6. Length 5: s0 = 1, s1 = 1 + 4 = 5, s2 = 4 + 2 × 11 = 26. Counts 1, 5, 26. Each row adds up to 2^n: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
7. Accepted strings of length 5 are those that end in the final state s2: 26. Check: the 6 strings with no ab are b^i a^j, and 32 − 6 = 26.

**Answer:** 26 strings (all strings of length 5 that contain ab).

steps.caption: The state is the remainder mod 3 of the bits read so far. Reading bit b turns remainder r into (2r + b) mod 3. Start in r0 with input 1001.
Read 1: r0 goes to r1, because (2*0 + 1) mod 3 = 1.
Read 0: r1 goes to r2, because (2*1 + 0) mod 3 = 2.
Read 0: r2 goes to r1, because (2*2 + 0) mod 3 = 4 mod 3 = 1.
Read 1: r1 goes to r0, because (2*1 + 1) mod 3 = 0.

set.text: run: r0 r1 r2 r1 r0

steps.caption: The string is used up and the run ended in r0, a final state, so 1001 is accepted. Check: 1001 is 9 in binary, and 9 = 3 * 3.

scenes.title: Tracing aab on an ε-NFA with sets of states

steps.caption: An ε-NFA may also move along ε arrows (dashed) without reading a symbol. We track the set S of states we could be in. Input: aab, start state A.
Start with the ε-closure of A: A goes to B on ε, so S = {A, B}.
Read a: A has no a-move, B goes to B and C. Then close under ε: C goes to D. S = {B, C, D}.
Read a: B goes to B and C, D goes to D, and C has no a-move. The closure adds nothing new. S = {B, C, D}.
Read b: only C has a b-move, to C. Then close under ε: C goes to D. S = {C, D}.
The string is used up and S = {C, D} contains the final state D, so aab is accepted. Without that last closure you would see only {C} and wrongly reject.

scenes.title: Subset construction table for a 3-state NFA

steps.caption: The NFA has states 0, 1, 2 (start 0, final 2). In the subset construction each DFA state is a SET of NFA states. We begin with the start set {0}.
From {0}: on a, state 0 goes to 0 and 1, so the set {0,1}. On b, state 0 goes to 0, so {0}. {0,1} is new.
From {0,1}: on a, 0 gives 0,1 and 1 gives 2, so {0,1,2}. On b, 0 gives 0 and 1 gives 2, so {0,2}. Two new sets.
From {0,1,2}: on a we get {0,1,2} again (state 2 has no moves). On b we get {0,2}. Nothing new appears.
From {0,2}: on a we get {0,1}, on b we get {0}. Both are known, so no new row is needed and the table is closed.
A set is final if it contains the NFA final state 2: {0,1,2} and {0,2}. Only 4 of the 2^3 = 8 possible subsets were reachable, so the DFA has 4 states.

scenes.title: Merging equivalent states by partition refinement

steps.caption: This DFA has 5 states. Two states can merge only if no string tells them apart. Start with the coarsest split: final states {C, E} (class F) versus the rest {A, B, D} (class N).
For each state, write the classes its a-move and b-move lead to. A: (N,N). B: (F,N). D: (F,N). C and E: (F,F).
Inside class N, A differs from B and D: A's a-move stays in N, theirs go to F. So N splits into {A} (class P) and {B, D} (class Q). {C, E} stays together as R.
Check again with the new classes. A: (Q,P). B: (R,Q). D: (R,Q). C: (R,R). E: (R,R). States in the same class have the same pair, so nothing splits.
The partition is stable. B and D are equivalent, and so are C and E. Merge each pair into one state.
The minimal DFA has 3 states: {A}, {B,D}, {C,E}. It counts the a's up to 2: strings with at least two a's.

scenes.title: Building the language of (ab + b)*a piece by piece

objects.text:
ε, b, ab, bb,
abb, bab, bbb, …

a, ba, aba, bba,
abba, baba, bbba, …

steps.caption: Read R = (ab + b)* a from the inside out. + means OR, * means 'repeat zero or more times', and writing two parts next to each other means 'then'.
The union ab + b is the set of two blocks: {ab, b}.
The star repeats blocks zero or more times, in any mix: ε (zero blocks), b, ab, bb, abb, bab, bbb, and so on.
Put an a after every string of the star part: a, ba, aba, bba, abba, baba, bbba, and so on. That is L(R).
Test two strings. abba = (ab)(b)(a) is in L(R). abab is not: it does not end in a, and every string of L(R) ends with the single trailing a.
In words: L(R) is the set of strings that end in a and contain no aa. Every a inside the blocks is followed by b, and only the final a is free.

set.text: ends in a, and no aa

scenes.title: Eliminating a state to get (b + ab*a)*

steps.caption: This DFA accepts strings with an even number of a's. State E (start, final) means 'even so far', O means 'odd so far'. We will remove O and keep the regex on the arrows.
Look at the detour E → O → E. It reads an a, then any number of b's (the loop on O), then an a. As a regex that is a b* a.
Remove state O and put the detour on E as a new loop labelled ab*a.

set.text: loops on E: b and ab*a

steps.caption: Two parallel loops merge into one with +. E now has a single loop labelled b + ab*a.
E is both the start and the only final state, so we go round that loop any number of times: (b + ab*a)*.
Check: baab = b, then a·ε·a, then b is in the language (two a's). ab has one a, so it is out. Brute force over all strings up to length 10 confirms the regex matches the DFA.

scenes.title: Hunting a witness between (ab)*a and a(ab)*

steps.caption: Are (ab)*a and a(ab)* the same language? Equal languages agree on every string. One string where they disagree proves they are different, so we hunt for a witness, shortest strings first.
Length 0 and 1: ε is in neither. a is in both: (ab)*a with zero repeats, a(ab)* with zero repeats.
Length 2: aa and ab are in neither expression. Both languages contain only a so far.
Length 3: aab = a·(ab) is in a(ab)* but not in (ab)*a, because that one must end in a. A witness: the two languages differ.
aba = (ab)·a is in (ab)*a but not in a(ab)*. Another witness, on the other side. One witness is enough.
So (ab)*a ≠ a(ab)*. Compare a(ba)*: it generates a, aba, ababa, the same strings as (ab)*a, and no string up to length 8 separates them. Those two are equal.

scenes.title: Complement of a DFA: swap the final states

steps.caption: L = strings that contain bb. This complete DFA has the single final state s2, which absorbs everything once bb has appeared.
Run abb on M: s0, s0, s1, s2. It ends in the final state s2, so abb is accepted. It does contain bb.

set.text: abb: s0 s0 s1 s2 = accept

steps.caption: Complement: keep every arrow and swap final with non-final. Now s0 and s1 are final, and s2 is not.
Run abb on the new machine: it still ends in s2, which is no longer final, so abb is rejected. That is right, because abb contains bb.
Run aba on the new machine: s0, s0, s1, s0. It ends in s0, which is now final, so aba is accepted. aba contains no bb.

set.text: aba: s0 s0 s1 s0 = accept

steps.caption: This works because the DFA is complete: every string ends somewhere. With a missing arrow the dead state is invisible and flipping would miss it. Closure under complement then gives intersection and difference by De Morgan.

set.text: complete DFA first, then flip finals

scenes.title: Product of an a-parity DFA and a b-parity DFA

steps.caption: Run D1 (even number of a's) and D2 (even number of b's) at the same time. A product state is a pair: (a-parity, b-parity), written e or o for even or odd. Start: both even, ee.
From ee: reading a flips only the first part, so oe. Reading b flips only the second part, so eo.
From oe: a gives ee, b gives oo.
From eo: a gives oo, b gives ee.
From oo: a gives eo, b gives oe. No new pairs appear: all 2 × 2 = 4 pairs are reachable.
Intersection (both even): the pair is final only if both parts are final, so just ee.
Union (at least one even): the pair is final if either part is final: ee, oe and eo. Same states and arrows, different finals.
